title: Valuation & Market Analysis
overview: This chapter covers value vs. price vs. cost, the principles of value, highest and best use, the appraisal process, New York appraiser licensing, and pricing a listing with a comparative market analysis (CMA). The exam hits hardest: adjust the comparable, never the subject; capitalize NOI, not cash flow; and in New York a CMA is never an appraisal.

Highest-and-best-use tests, in order: legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive
Approaches to value: sales comparison, cost, income
Kinds of accrued depreciation: physical deterioration, functional obsolescence, external obsolescence
Neighborhood life-cycle stages: growth, stability, decline, revitalization

Minimum closed comparable sales in a Fannie Mae appraisal; 3 to 6 is typical

Minimum time a supervisor must be state-certified; max 3 trainees at once
Continuing education per renewal: 7-hour USPAP plus valuation bias and fair housing course
Experience hours: licensed residential / certified residential / certified general. Assistants: none, no exam
Reg B appraisal copy: on completion or 3 business days pre-closing, whichever is earlier
Federal bank appraisal threshold for home loans since 2019; older books say $250,000

mustKnow: **Appraisal**: an unbiased, supported opinion of the value of defined rights as of an **effective date**. Federally related loans require a state licensed or certified appraiser.
**Valuation** is the process of estimating value; an **evaluation** studies utility or feasibility without necessarily estimating value.
In New York a **CMA** is an opinion of value and by law may never be called an **appraisal**; a real estate license carries no appraiser credential.
**Market value** is the **most probable** price, not the highest, after reasonable exposure, in cash or its equivalent, between informed parties under no duress, in an arm's-length sale.
**Price** is what a buyer actually paid; **cost** is what it takes to build; either can differ from value.
**Direct (hard) costs** are labor and materials; **indirect (soft) costs** are fees, permits, financing and administration.
**DUST**: demand (desire plus purchasing power), utility, scarcity and transferability must all exist.
**Substitution**: buyers pay no more than an equally desirable substitute costs; it drives the sales comparison approach.
**Regression** pulls the best house on the block down; **progression** pulls a modest house among better ones up.
**Contribution**: a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost.
**Anticipation** (value is the present worth of future benefits) underlies the income approach; **change** ties every value to a date.
**Highest and best use**: legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive. Analyze it as vacant and as improved.
Appraisal process: define the problem, set the scope of work, collect data, analyze (including highest and best use), value the land, apply the approaches, **reconcile**, report.
DOS licenses appraisers under **Executive Law Article 6-E**.

**Certified general** covers all property; certified residential covers 1–4 units of any value; licensed residential is capped by value and complexity; an assistant works only under a certified supervisor.
**USPAP** bans fees contingent on the value reported and requires competence. The Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation writes it.
**Appraiser independence**: no one may pressure an appraiser toward a value; asking through the lender to consider more comps or correct errors is allowed.
A **BPO** is a broker's price estimate for lenders (foreclosures, short sales); it can't be the primary basis of value for a mortgage to buy a principal home.
CMA data: solds show what buyers paid, **actives** show the competition, **expireds** show prices the market rejected.
Adjust the **comparable**, never the subject: comp better, subtract; comp poorer, add.
Transaction adjustments (financing, concessions, time) come before physical ones; use only **arm's-length** sales; the comp with the smallest **gross** adjustment usually gets the most weight.
Cost approach: **land + (cost new − accrued depreciation)**; land is never depreciated.
**Reproduction** cost = exact replica; **replacement** cost = equal utility with modern materials, the usual choice for older buildings.
Depreciation: physical (wear), **functional** (design or features inside the property, including overimprovement), **external** (outside the property, almost always incurable).
**Curable** means the cure costs no more than the value it adds.
**Age-life**: depreciation = cost new × effective age ÷ total economic life; use **effective**, not calendar, age.
PGI − vacancy and collection loss + other income = EGI; EGI − operating expenses = **NOI**; **value = NOI ÷ cap rate**.
NOI excludes **debt service**, tax depreciation, income taxes and capital improvements, but includes a market management fee and reserves for replacement.
Higher risk means a higher cap rate and a **lower** value.
**GRM** = price ÷ monthly rent; **GIM** = price ÷ annual gross income. Some questions give an annual GRM for annual rent. Match the periods; multipliers ignore vacancy and expenses.
**Reconciliation** weighs the indications rather than simply averaging them: sales comparison for homes, income for investment property, cost for new or special-purpose buildings.

traps.trap: A salesperson may call a CMA an appraisal if no fee is charged.
traps.truth: A CMA is never an appraisal, paid or free, so 'free home appraisal' flyers are improper. Only credential holders may use the state appraiser titles (Exec. Law §160-b).

traps.trap: When the comparable has a feature the subject lacks, add its value.
traps.truth: Subtract, because the comp is superior: a $350,000 comp with a $15,000 garage the subject lacks adjusts to $335,000. Adjust the comp, never the subject.

traps.trap: Depreciate the whole property, land included.
traps.truth: Depreciation comes off the cost new of the improvements only; land is added back at full value.

traps.trap: Mortgage payments are an operating expense.
traps.truth: Debt service is excluded from NOI. NOI − debt service is before-tax cash flow; the income approach capitalizes NOI, not cash flow, to value the property.

traps.trap: Curable means the defect can physically be repaired.
traps.truth: Curable is an economic test: the cure costs no more than the value it adds. An $85,000 foundation repair that adds $30,000 is incurable.

traps.trap: A poor floor plan is external obsolescence.
traps.truth: Problems inside the property are functional obsolescence. External obsolescence comes from outside, such as a landfill or a plant closing.

traps.trap: Market value is the highest price a buyer might pay.
traps.truth: Market value is the most probable price. One specially motivated buyer's higher figure is investment value.

traps.trap: The age-life method uses the building's actual age.
traps.truth: Age-life uses effective age, which reflects condition and renovation. A gutted and rebuilt 45-year-old house might have an effective age of 15.
Reconciliation weighs each indication by reliability and relevance. A simple average gives weak data an equal say.

traps.trap: A higher cap rate means a higher value.
traps.truth: A higher cap rate means a lower value: $120,000 of NOI is worth $2,000,000 at 6% but only $1,500,000 at 8%.

traps.trap: A monthly GRM can be applied to annual rent.
traps.truth: Match the periods: monthly GRM × monthly rent, annual GIM × annual income. Otherwise the answer is off by a factor of 12.

traps.trap: Comps must be under 6 months old, and every year of age knocks $1,000 off value.
traps.truth: The DOS outline uses a 12-month look-back, and every adjustment must come from market evidence. Neither the 6-month nor the $1,000 figure is a rule.

traps.trap: Any licensed appraiser can supervise an appraiser assistant.
traps.truth: The supervisor must be state-certified for at least 3 years and approved by DOS, with no more than 3 trainees at a time. A licensed residential appraiser can't supervise.
Combining parcels is assemblage; plottage is the extra value the combined parcel has.

formulas.name: Adjusted comparable price
formulas.formula: Comp price − comp's extra features + subject features the comp lacks

formulas.name: Market-conditions (time) adjustment
formulas.formula: Comp price × (1 + monthly rate × months since sale)

formulas.name: Age-life depreciation
formulas.formula: Cost new × effective age ÷ total economic life

formulas.name: Index method
formulas.formula: Original cost × current index ÷ original index

formulas.name: NOI
formulas.formula: PGI − vacancy and collection loss + other income − operating expenses

formulas.name: Value (income approach)
formulas.formula: Value = NOI ÷ cap rate; rate = NOI ÷ value

formulas.formula: GRM = price ÷ monthly rent; value = monthly rent × GRM

formulas.name: Weighted reconciliation
formulas.formula: Sum of each indication × its weight

sections.heading: Appraisal, valuation, evaluation, price and cost
sections.intro: Many questions turn on picking the right word, so start with the Department of State (DOS) vocabulary.
points: An **appraisal** is an unbiased, supported estimate of the value of an identified interest in real estate as of a stated date. It can also address the property's nature, quality or utility.
Federally related loans require a state licensed or certified appraiser.
**Valuation** is the process of estimating value as of a given date. An appraisal is one kind of valuation; a CMA is a less formal one.

An **evaluation** studies utility, feasibility, marketability or highest and best use without necessarily producing a value. Bank regulators also use 'evaluation' for a simplified estimate on some smaller loans; on the exam, use the syllabus meaning.

**Price** is what one buyer and seller agreed to in one deal. **Cost** is the total outlay to build, including the contractor's and developer's overhead and profit. Either can sit above or below value.

head: Term
What it is
Exam clue
rows: Unbiased, supported opinion of value as of an effective date
Credentialed appraisers follow the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP)
The builder could build it today for $380,000
Architect, engineering, appraisal and legal fees; permits; construction-loan interest; lease-up; administration

sections.heading: Market value and other types of value
points: DOS defines **market value** as the most probable price, as of a specific date, in cash or its equivalent, for which the specified property rights should sell after reasonable exposure in a competitive market.
The sale must meet all conditions requisite to a fair sale: buyer and seller act prudently, knowledgeably and in their own interest, and neither is under undue duress.
Key pieces: **probable**, not the highest price or the first offer; a specific date; and **cash equivalent**, so special financing and concessions are adjusted out.
The value is for the specified rights after **reasonable exposure** before the sale. Marketing time is the separate estimate of how long a sale would take afterward.
Fair-sale conditions: a broad market, wide publicity, time, knowledge and no duress.
It assumes an **arm's-length** sale between unrelated parties; family, related-company and forced sales are poor evidence.
**Market price** is what a property actually sold for, which may or may not equal market value.

Exam clue

sections.heading: Elements, forces and principles of value
sections.intro: Principle questions usually tell a short story and ask which principle it shows.
points: All four **elements of value** (DUST) must exist: demand, utility, scarcity and transferability. Immobility, indestructibility and uniqueness describe land itself, not value.
Demand means **effective demand**: desire backed by purchasing power.

Four **forces** affect value (PEGS): physical (location, topography, access), economic (jobs, incomes, interest rates), governmental (zoning, taxes, codes) and social (population, household size, tastes).

The protected traits of a neighborhood's residents are never a value factor. The federal Fair Housing Act expressly covers appraising, and New York's Human Rights Law bars discrimination in real estate transactions.
Under the principle of change, neighborhoods follow a **life cycle**: growth, stability, decline, and sometimes revitalization.

Exam clue
rows: No one pays more than an equally desirable substitute costs

300 new condos, same buyers, prices fall

An inferior property is pulled up by better neighbors
A cottage on a street of large, expensive homes

A rail station raises values; a landfill lowers them

A mansion squeezed onto a tiny lot

A second bath pays; a fifth may not

sections.heading: Highest and best use and site valuation
points: **Highest and best use** is the reasonably probable use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive, **tested in that order**.
A use barred by zoning fails no matter how profitable. Among uses passing the first three tests, the highest-value one wins.
Test it **as vacant** and as improved. If the site's value as vacant, minus demolition cost, exceeds the property's value as improved, the existing building is an **interim use**.
**Site valuation**: land is usually valued by comparing vacant-land sales, adjusted for location, size, shape, frontage, topography, utilities and zoning. Usable area matters more than gross acreage.
Other land methods: **allocation** applies a typical land-to-total ratio; **extraction** takes the sale price minus the depreciated improvements.
**Assemblage** is combining parcels; **plottage** is the extra value the combined parcel has.

example.title: Worked example: as vacant vs. as improved
steps: An old house on a lot rezoned for apartments is worth $680,000 as improved.
The cleared lot would sell for $900,000, and demolition costs $60,000, so it nets $840,000 as vacant.
Answer: $840,000 beats $680,000, so the house is an interim use and redevelopment is the highest and best use.

sections.heading: The appraisal process
sections.intro: Expect questions on the first step and on the order of the steps.
points: Step one is **defining the problem**: client and intended use, the property and the rights appraised, the type of value, the **effective date** and any assumptions.
Rights matter. **Fee simple** is ownership free of leases.
The **leased fee** is the landlord's interest in leased property; the **leasehold** is the tenant's. A building locked into a below-market lease can be worth less as a leased fee.
The **effective date** is the date the value applies to. Values go stale as markets change; New York law sets no expiration date, though lenders and agencies limit how old an appraisal may be.

USPAP's report options are the **Appraisal Report** and the **Restricted Appraisal Report**; home loans typically use forms such as the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR). An appraisal is not a home inspection.

example.title: Worked example: the steps in order for a leased office building
steps: Define the problem: lender client, leased fee interest, market value, effective date June 1.
Set the scope of work: inspection, lease review, sales and rent comparables.
Collect general data (region, neighborhood, trends) and specific data (the subject and the comparables).
Analyze the market and highest and best use, as vacant and as improved.
Value the land from vacant-site sales.
Apply the approaches: income first, supported by sales comparison and cost.
Reconcile, giving the income approach the most weight.
Answer: the last step is the report, signed with the appraiser's credential title and number.

sections.heading: Appraiser licensing, standards and independence
sections.intro: Real estate licensees and appraisers are separate professions under separate laws.
points: The Department of State licenses and certifies New York appraisers under **Executive Law Article 6-E**, with the **State Board of Real Estate Appraisal**.
A broker or salesperson license under Real Property Law Article 12-A is not an appraiser credential.

Only credential holders may use the titles 'state certified real estate appraiser', 'state licensed real estate appraiser' or 'state licensed real estate appraiser assistant', or call an appraisal 'certified' or 'licensed' (Exec. Law §160-b).
Article 6-E is a title law. It doesn't bar uncredentialed appraising (§160-b(2)), but federally related loans need a credentialed appraiser, and a licensee's CMA may never be called an appraisal.
Reports must show the credential title and number (§160-r).
**FIRREA** requires credentialed appraisers for federally related loans above set thresholds (Title XI of the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act, 1989).
FIRREA makes **USPAP** the standard. USPAP is written by the Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation.
The federal bank appraisal threshold for home loans is **$400,000** since 2019; older books say $250,000. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA and VA keep their own appraisal rules.
USPAP **Ethics Rule**: be impartial and never discriminate. Never take a fee contingent on a predetermined result, the value reported or the loan closing.
Disclosure doesn't cure a contingent fee, and New York bans such fees too (Exec. Law §160-y).
USPAP **Competency Rule**: be competent. If not, disclose the gap to the client before accepting, become competent and describe how in the report; or decline.
Holding the right credential doesn't by itself prove competence for an unfamiliar property type.

**Appraiser independence**: on a loan secured by a consumer's principal dwelling, no lender, broker, agent or other interested person may pressure the appraiser toward a value, even unsuccessfully (Truth in Lending Act §129E; Regulation Z §1026.42).
Allowed: asking through the lender to consider more comps, explain the conclusion or correct errors.

**Regulation B**: on a first-lien dwelling loan the applicant gets a free copy of each appraisal promptly on completion or 3 business days before closing, whichever is earlier, unless the applicant waives the timing. The lender orders the appraisal; the buyer usually pays for it.

After a **low appraisal**, the buyer adds cash, the price is renegotiated, the lender is asked to reconsider with better comps, or the buyer uses an appraisal or mortgage contingency if the contract has one.
Since January 1, 2026, New York appraisers must take a Valuation Bias and Fair Housing Laws and Regulations course.
That course is 8 hours in qualifying education, at least 7 hours for the first renewal and 4 for later renewals.
DOS doesn't count a licensee's CMAs as appraisal experience.

sections.heading: CMA vs. appraisal vs. BPO
points: A **comparative market analysis (CMA)** compares the subject with recent sales, active listings and expired listings to recommend a price range.
By law a CMA may never be referred to as an appraisal (DOS syllabus).
A **broker price opinion (BPO)** is a broker's estimate of probable selling price, often from an exterior-only look.
Lenders or investors use BPOs for foreclosed property (REO, real estate owned), short sales or portfolio reviews.
Federal law bars using a BPO as the primary basis of value for a mortgage to buy a consumer's principal dwelling (12 U.S.C. §3355).
A client who wants an 'appraisal' for a divorce or estate should get a CMA clearly labeled as not an appraisal, plus a referral to a state licensed or certified appraiser.

CMA
BPO
Appraisal
rows: Appraiser; licensed or certified for federally related loans

sections.heading: Preparing a CMA and pricing a listing
points: **Data**: sale date, verified price, days on market, financing and concessions, plus size, rooms, baths, garage, age, condition and location, from the multiple listing service (MLS) and public records.
**Comparable sales**: the DOS outline uses sales from the last 12 months. Newer and more similar is better, and older sales need a market-conditions adjustment.
**Active listings** are the competition (asking, not selling, prices); **expired** listings show prices the market rejected, an upper limit.
Also weigh buyer appeal, market position, assets and drawbacks, area market conditions, recommended terms and the resulting **market value range**.
The salesperson recommends; the seller sets the list price.
The **salesperson's role**: competence, diligence (follow up and track competition), documentation (showings and feedback) and effective communication with the seller.
Never inflate a CMA to win a listing.

example.title: Worked example: from CMA data to a price range
steps: Adjusted solds indicate $398,000, $404,000 and $411,000.
Actives at $419,000 and $425,000 have sat 70 days, and a similar listing at $440,000 expired.
Answer: recommend about $398,000 to $411,000; listing at $440,000 would repeat the expired listing's mistake.

sections.heading: Sales comparison approach
sections.intro: The main approach for homes, condos and vacant land, built on substitution and contribution.
points: Use at least 3 recent, nearby, similar, closed **arm's-length** sales; a family or forced sale doesn't qualify. **Bracket** the subject with comps both larger and smaller.
Adjust the **comparable**, never the subject: a superior comp gets a subtraction; an inferior comp gets an addition.
Order: transaction adjustments first (property rights, financing terms and seller concessions, conditions of sale, then market conditions over time), then location and physical features.
**Paired sales** isolate a feature: identical homes at $415,000 with a finished basement and $396,000 without imply $19,000 for it.
Adjust size at the market's rate per added square foot, not the comp's overall price per square foot.
**Net** adjustment nets the pluses and minuses; **gross** adjustment totals them ignoring sign. The comp with the smallest gross adjustment is usually the most reliable.

head: Situation
Adjust the comparable
Example
rows: Comp has a feature the subject lacks
Comp lacks a feature the subject has
Add the missing area at the market rate
A mother sells to her son below market

example.title: Worked example: adjusting one comparable
steps: The comp sold 6 months ago for $410,000 with a $10,000 seller concession (not typical). Prices rose 0.5% a month. The comp has an extra half bath worth $6,000 and lacks the subject's central air, worth $7,000.
Remove the concession: $410,000 − $10,000 = $400,000.
Superior half bath, subtract: $412,000 − $6,000 = $406,000.
Missing central air, add: $406,000 + $7,000 = $413,000.
Answer: $413,000. The net adjustment is only +$3,000, but the gross adjustment is $35,000.

sections.heading: Cost approach and estimating cost new
points: **Value = land + cost new of improvements − accrued depreciation.** Land is valued separately, usually by sales comparison, and is never depreciated.

**Reproduction cost** is an exact replica with the same materials (a 1920s bank's marble columns). **Replacement cost** is equal utility with modern materials; it is usually lower and preferred for older buildings.
The most common way to estimate cost new is the **square-foot** method: area × cost per sq ft. Price garages at their own rate and split irregular shapes into rectangles.
**Unit-in-place** method: installed cost per component, such as foundation per linear foot and roofing per 100-sq-ft square.
**Quantity survey** method: every material and labor hour, the most detailed.
**Index** method: original cost × current index ÷ original index.
Best for new construction and **special-purpose** property that rarely sells and earns no rent (churches, schools, firehouses). It can't value a vacant lot by itself and is weak for old buildings.

example.title: Worked example: cost approach with age-life depreciation
steps: Facts: land $100,000; 2,000 sq ft of living area at $200; a 500 sq ft garage at $40; effective age 10 years; total economic life 50 years.
Answer: $436,000. Depreciating the land too gives $416,000, and forgetting the land gives $336,000.

sections.heading: Depreciation: physical, functional and external
sections.intro: In appraisal, accrued depreciation is any loss in value from cost new. It is not the tax deduction investors take.
points: **Physical deterioration**: wear, weather, neglect or damage, such as peeling paint, worn carpet or a settled foundation.

**Functional obsolescence**: design or features inside the property that the market dislikes (a poor layout, too few baths, a walk-through bedroom, a dated kitchen), including a **superadequacy** or overimprovement.

**External (economic) obsolescence**: causes outside the property lines, such as a landfill, a highway, a plant closing or nearby rezoning. It can hit a brand-new house and is almost always **incurable**.
**Curable** means the cure costs no more than the value it adds: a $6,000 fix adding $9,000 is curable; an $85,000 fix adding $30,000 is not.
**Effective age** reflects condition; **chronological age** is calendar age.
Remaining economic life = total life − effective age. The annual straight-line rate = 100% ÷ total life (40 years = 2.5%). Cost new = depreciated value ÷ (1 − depreciation %).
Tax depreciation is a deduction, not a measure of market value. It commonly runs 27½ years for residential rental buildings and 39 for nonresidential.

head: Type
Cause
Examples
Curable?
rows: Old roof, worn carpet, cracked foundation
One bath for four bedrooms, 1970s kitchen
Eight-car garage in a starter-home area

example.title: Worked example: breakdown method
steps: Replacement cost new $400,000; land $90,000. Estimates: worn roof and siding $30,000 (physical); one bath for four bedrooms $18,000 (functional); new highway noise $25,000 (external).
Total accrued depreciation: $30,000 + $18,000 + $25,000 = $73,000.
Answer: $90,000 + ($400,000 − $73,000) = $417,000. Skipping the external item would wrongly give $442,000.

sections.heading: Income approach: NOI and capitalization
sections.intro: Investors buy income, so this approach converts net operating income into value. It rests on anticipation.
points: **Potential gross income (PGI)** is all rent at full occupancy for a year (12 units × $1,450 × 12 = $208,800).
Subtract vacancy and collection loss and add other income (laundry, parking) to get **effective gross income (EGI)**.
EGI − operating expenses = **net operating income (NOI)**.

Operating expenses are fixed (taxes, insurance), variable (utilities, repairs) or **reserves for replacement** (roofs, boilers, appliances). Include a market management fee even if the owner self-manages.
Exclude **debt service**, tax depreciation, income taxes and capital improvements.
NOI − debt service = **before-tax cash flow**, the owner's return after financing. The income approach capitalizes NOI, not cash flow.
**IRV**: value = NOI ÷ cap rate; a comparable sale's rate = NOI ÷ price ($168,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 7%); NOI = value × rate.
Riskier income gets a higher cap rate and a lower value. Watch decimals: 8.5% is 0.085.

head: Item
In NOI?
Why
rows: Included even if the owner self-manages
Spread the cost of short-lived items
Depend on the owner's tax situation

example.title: Worked example: from rent roll to value
steps: Less 5% vacancy ($12,000), plus $6,000 laundry income: EGI = $234,000.
Operating expenses: taxes $40,000 + insurance $9,000 + utilities and repairs $25,000 + management $11,700 + reserves $4,300 = $90,000.
NOI = $234,000 − $90,000 = $144,000; the $100,000 mortgage payment is ignored.
Answer: $144,000 ÷ 0.08 = $1,800,000 (at 9%, only $1,600,000). Subtracting the mortgage first ($44,000 ÷ 0.08 = $550,000) is the classic wrong answer.

sections.heading: Gross rent and gross income multipliers
points: **Gross rent multiplier (GRM)** = price ÷ monthly rent, used for single-family homes and small rentals. **Gross income multiplier (GIM)** = price ÷ annual gross income, used for larger residential and commercial property.
Derive the multiplier from comparable sales, then value = the subject's rent × the multiplier, with matching periods (a monthly GRM of 180 equals an annual multiplier of 15).
The weakness: gross figures ignore differences in vacancy and expenses, so two buildings with equal rent get equal value even if one costs far more to run.

example.title: Worked example: GRM and GIM
steps: The subject rents for $2,100 a month: $2,100 × 150 = $315,000.
A commercial building grossing $150,000 a year at a market GIM of 8: $150,000 × 8 = $1,200,000.
Answer: $315,000 and $1,200,000. Applying the monthly GRM to annual rent ($25,200 × 150 = $3,780,000) is the trap.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and choosing the approach
points: Reconciliation weighs each indication by the quality of its data and its relevance to the property; it is not an average.
Owner-occupied homes: sales comparison gets the most weight. Investment property: the income approach. New or special-purpose property with few sales and no rent: the cost approach.
The final value is usually rounded and stated as of the effective date.

head: Approach
Best for
Weak when
Formula
rows: Few sales or a unique property
Old buildings; a vacant lot alone
Rental homes (GRM); larger rentals and commercial (GIM)

example.title: Worked example: weighted reconciliation
